speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To avoid this, MINDEF’s reply will, therefore, separately address three distinct issues within their questions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is important to emphasise even though they are somewhat related, these are three distinct issues.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In my reply, it will also be clear that the general principles Singapore adhere to govern our practices and specific protocols in response to all countries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, Singapore respects the rights of military aircraft and ships to conduct passage and training over areas and waters in accordance with international law, and this includes the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the basis upon which the Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF) aircraft conduct flights and training, whether it is in the South China Sea or other regions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is also the basis for the conduct of exercises in the South China Sea, the ones that Singapore does bilaterally and in multilateral exercises.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, for example, Exercise Commando Sling which is between the SAF and the US Air Force, and the Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training (CARAT) Exercise between the SAF and the US Navy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members may remember that we held a multilateral exercise in 2016 and this was involving navies of the ADMM-Plus countries, which sailed from Brunei to Singapore through the South China Sea, and exercised together en route.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You may also remember that during this year's Committee of Supply, I had also informed Members of this House that the South China Sea will see an increase in military activity from other countries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Earlier this year, the French Navy deployed its ships to the South China Sea.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Later this year, the UK will send the Queen Elizabeth Carrier Strike Group with its fighter aircraft F35Bs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Germans too intend to deploy a frigate to the South China Sea, the first time in almost 20 years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Apart from international law and UNCLOS, countries that conduct military activities in these areas have to act in accordance with ASEAN instruments that they have signed on to, such as the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I think it is instructive to quote from some of the phrases that these countries have agreed to in this treaty.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This treaty calls for "mutual respect for the independence, sovereignty, equality, territorial integrity and national identity of all nations", as well as for signatories not to "participate in any activity which shall constitute a threat to the political and economic stability, sovereignty or territorial integrity" of one another.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have dealt with the first issue in terms of rights of military training; let me deal with the second issue.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As distinct from military activity, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) appoints a civilian authority to manage the air space of each FIR.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And this authority is designated as the Air Traffic Services (ATS) Authority.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The role of the ATS Authority is to ensure safe and efficient flow of air traffic, mostly civilian, within its FIR.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this role, it does not act as a watchdog over disputed areas nor should that authority adopt a partisan role on behalf of any party or for itself.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Civilian aircraft must file flight plans when going through the FIR of an ATS Authority.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, state aircraft, which includes military aircraft, are not required to file flight plans under international law, and this includes the Convention on International Civil Aviation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: State aircraft are also not obliged to contact the ATS Authority so long as they fly with due regard for the safety of other aircraft.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Nevertheless, some militaries, including the RSAF, do file flight plans and contact the ATS Authority of that FIR, even when they are not legally required to do so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The RSAF routinely adopts this practice, primarily to assist the ATS Authority in coordinating and de-conflicting RSAF flights from civilian aircraft as part of their responsibility for operating with due care.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: ICAO has appointed the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) as the ATS Authority for the Singapore FIR.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this capacity, CAAS has gained an international reputation for managing the Singapore FIR in a safe, orderly, impartial and expeditious manner.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have already mentioned that state aircraft are not required to do so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Nevertheless, had the PLAAF required air traffic services, it could have established communications with CAAS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Giam’s question also confuses the role of CAAS as the ATS Authority for the Singapore FIR with the role of the SAF to defend Singapore’s own territorial airspace.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We should be clear that the RSAF has no mandate nor any role in the management of the Singapore FIR, which is carried out by CAAS, a civilian authority appointed by ICAO.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Singapore is a small country with a high population density and, therefore, more vulnerable to air threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF accordingly maintains air defence units at high alert.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The RSAF conducts 24/7 surveillance of our skies through both ground-based radars and aerial reconnaissance to detect unknown or suspicious aircraft that are close enough to pose a potential threat.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since state aircraft are not required to file flight plans when entering our FIR, how does Singapore ensure that these aircraft do not have hostile intent?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand that there is no requirement for them to file these flight plans, but do other countries, by convention, file their flight plans for their state aircraft and is this incident the only time that no flight plans were filed when entering the FIR?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Again, Mr Speaker, I think it is useful not to conscribe the question and direct it to any one country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It does not serve our foreign policy; it does not reflect our desire to be principled and neutral.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, again, the answer is with regard to any country and I think we must ask relevant questions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do you determine whether a particular aircraft of any country is friend or foe?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And that is the job of the RSAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you have mistaken a friend for a foe, there can be catastrophic consequences.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And as Members will remember, there are a number of incidents in previous years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: One was a private aircraft that got lost.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And, of course, I suppose seeing an F-16 next to you is, for some, comforting, and it was gently guided to land in a safe area.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There have been other instances which RSAF must use its judgement and there are strict protocols.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These relate to what we call aerial threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Giam asked whether other militaries – I presume he was asking that – file flight plans.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many countries do not file flight plans or contact the ATS Authority.
